analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare- and Medicaid-funded hospitals to offer emergency contraception to rape survivors.
analysis.headline: The bill won 104 cosponsors, including 5 Republicans, but never received a hearing or vote and died in committee at the end of the 110th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made Medicare and Medicaid funding conditional: any hospital drawing those federal funds would have to give rape survivors accurate information about emergency contraception, offer it to them, provide it on request, and not deny it to women who cannot pay. It was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees, never moved again, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.who_benefits: Women treated at hospitals after a sexual assault. The bill's own findings cite an estimated 25,000 to 32,000 pregnancies a year from rape or incest and note that surveys show many hospitals do not routinely offer emergency contraception, so survivors often leave without the option [S3]. Because emergency contraception works best the sooner it is taken, guaranteeing it at the hospital removes the delay of hunting for a pharmacy [S3]. Women who cannot pay are explicitly protected from being turned away [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Every hospital drawing Medicare funds, and every state drawing Medicaid hospital funding, must provide rape survivors medically accurate, unbiased information about emergency contraception, offer it, and supply it at the hospital on request [S2][S3].
Hospitals may not deny these services to a woman because she or her family cannot pay [S2].

The bill's findings state that surveys show many hospitals do not routinely provide emergency contraception to sexual assault patients, and that medical groups including the American Medical Association and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists call offering it after an assault the standard of care [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals that receive Medicare and Medicaid funds. They would have to stock and dispense emergency contraception and absorb the cost for patients who cannot pay, and any hospital refusing to comply would risk its federal funding [S2][S3]. Religiously affiliated hospital systems, which oppose emergency contraception on moral grounds, would have to choose between their practice and federal funds, since the bill contains no conscience exemption.

drawbacks.text: The bill attaches a funding condition to Medicare and Medicaid rather than writing a direct rule, so a hospital that declines for religious or policy reasons would lose federal funds entirely — a heavy penalty with no conscience exemption or hardship waiver [S2][S3].

Hospitals bear the cost of stocking and dispensing emergency contraception without charge to patients who cannot pay, an expense that is small per case but applies to every Medicare-participating hospital nationwide [S2][S3].
Survivors must still reach a hospital for the mandate to apply; the bill does nothing for women treated outside a hospital setting [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and targeted: a rape survivor who arrives at a hospital would get the option of emergency contraception at the moment it is most effective, without having to know to ask or pay out of pocket. The costs are real but narrow — a stocking and dispensing burden on hospitals and a genuine conflict with religious hospitals that receive large Medicare and Medicaid funding. A more negotiated version could have included a conscience mechanism; as written, the all-or-nothing funding condition was the strongest honest objection. On balance the human stakes for survivors substantially outweigh the compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees and then to their health subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 12, 2007 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, the House Ways and Means Committee [S1][S5].
Both committees referred it to their health subcommittees in January and February 2007; no further action was taken on the bill for the remainder of the 110th Congress [S5].
The bill gathered 104 cosponsors, 99 Democrats and 5 Republicans, but never reached the House floor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, particularly those unwilling to provide emergency contraception, kept their existing practices and their federal funding without any new conditions; rape survivors gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals that kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic — 99 of 104 — though five Republicans, including moderates like Reps. Kirk, Shays, and Castle, signed on.

industries.industry: Hospitals, including religiously affiliated hospital systems
industries.note: The bill conditions Medicare and Medicaid funding on stocking and dispensing emergency contraception to rape survivors without charge to those who cannot pay. Hospitals that refused on religious or policy grounds would have risked losing federal funds, so their institutional interest in the bill ran against survivors' access to care.

A nationwide hospital mandate would make emergency contraception a standard item stocked and dispensed at hospitals, creating a new institutional sales channel. That interest runs alongside survivors' access to the product.
